questions.question: A particle moves in a circle with uniform speed. Which statement is correct?
questions.answer: Constant speed means constant $K=\frac12mv^2$. The net force is centripetal (perpendicular to the motion) and the momentum changes direction.
options: The kinetic energy of the particle is constant.
The net force on the particle is in the same direction as the direction of motion.
The momentum of the particle is constant.
The displacement of the particle is in the direction of the net force.

questions.question: The diagram shows two positions, X and Y, at different heights on the surface of the Earth. Which row correctly compares, at X with Y, the gravitational potential energy (of equal masses) and the angular velocity?
questions.answer: X is higher, so GPE is greater there. Both points rotate once per day with the Earth, so $\omega$ is the same.
options: GPE at X greater; angular velocity at X greater
GPE at X greater; angular velocity the same
GPE at X greater; angular velocity at X smaller
GPE the same; angular velocity the same

questions.question: Which graph correctly shows the relationship between the gravitational force $F$ between two masses and the distance $r$ between them?
questions.answer: $F=\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$, so $F$ against $1/r^2$ is a straight line through the origin.

questions.question: Some energy levels of the hydrogen atom are shown. Electrons are excited to the $-0.85$ eV level. How many different photon frequencies are possible in the emission spectrum?
Which statement about radioactive decay is true?
questions.answer: $t_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$.
options: The half-life of a radioactive isotope depends on the amount of material present.
The activity of a radioactive isotope is inversely proportional to its decay constant.
The half-life increases as more of the isotope decays.
The half-life is inversely proportional to the decay constant.

questions.question: In experiments supervised by Rutherford, a very thin gold foil was bombarded with alpha particles. Which observation was correct?
questions.answer: Most passed almost undeflected and a very few were deflected through large angles, implying a small, dense, positive nucleus.
options: All of the α particles passed through without significant deflection.
All of the α particles passed through and were deflected through large angles.
Most of the α particles passed through with negligible deflection but some were deflected through large angles.
The α particles were linearly polarised after passing through the foil.

questions.question: When electrons of suitable energy travel through a thin layer of graphite, a pattern of concentric circles is produced on a screen. This pattern is evidence for:
questions.answer: The rings are a diffraction pattern, which is a wave property.
options: the wave nature of the electron
the nuclear model of the atom
the particle nature of the electron

questions.question: The energy released by the Hiroshima bomb is given as equivalent to $9.0\times10^{26}$ MeV. What mass was converted into energy?
Which is a correct statement about Hubble's discovery?
questions.answer: Hubble's law: $v=H_0d$.
options: The recessional velocity of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance from the Earth.
The recessional velocity of a galaxy is inversely proportional to its distance from the Earth.
The faster a spiral galaxy's rotational speed, the more luminous it is.
The faster a spiral galaxy's rotational speed, the less luminous it is.

questions.question: Light of intensity $I_0$ passes through a sheet of Polaroid, with its axis vertical, which reduces the intensity to $0.5I_0$. The light then passes through a second parallel sheet. At what angle to the first axis should the second axis be placed to reduce the intensity to 30% of $I_0$?
questions.answer: $0.3I_0=0.5I_0\cos^2\theta$, so $\cos^2\theta=\frac35$.

questions.question: What is the magnitude of the momentum (in kg m s$^{-1}$) of an electron travelling at $0.8c$?
The length of a spaceship is measured to be exactly one third of its rest length as it passes an observing station. What is the speed of the spaceship as determined by the station?
The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons was plotted against frequency for four metals. Which lists the metals in order of increasing work function?
questions.answer: $\phi=hf_0$ increases with the threshold frequency (the $x$-intercept): K < Mg < Zn < Pt.

questions.question: Which expression gives the charge on an oil drop balanced in a Millikan oil drop experiment (symbols have their usual meanings)?
questions.answer: $QV/d=mg$.

questions.question: Which nuclear equation correctly represents beta-minus decay?
questions.answer: A neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino (conserving lepton number).

questions.question: Light of a particular wavelength is incident on a metal and electrons are emitted. To produce more electrons per unit time with less kinetic energy per electron, which changes are required?
questions.answer: Greater intensity gives more photons per second; longer wavelength gives less energy per photon.

questions.question: After a DC motor is switched on, its speed gradually increases. Which quantity also increases?
questions.answer: Back emf is proportional to the rate of change of flux, so it rises with speed (reducing current and torque).

questions.question: The diagram shows a type of generator. Which identifies the type of generator and the relative magnitude of the induced emf at the position shown?
questions.answer: Two complete slip rings give AC. The plane of the coil is parallel to the field, so the rate of change of flux and the emf are maximum.

questions.question: An electron travelling in the positive $x$-direction enters a uniform electric field between two plates (diagram). Which pair of graphs shows the acceleration and velocity of the electron in the $y$-direction while in the field?
questions.answer: The top plate is positive (long line of the cell), so the electron has a constant acceleration in $+y$ and $v_y$ increases linearly from zero.

questions.question: The graph shows how the magnetic flux through a loop varies with time, with times P, Q, R, S and T marked. Which correctly compares the magnitudes of the induced emf at these times (largest emf; smallest non-zero emf; zero emf)?
questions.answer: The emf equals the magnitude of the gradient: steep at Q, gentle at S, zero at P, R and T.
options: S; Q; P, R and T
Q; S; P, R and T

questions.question:
A bullet is fired at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal with speed $200$ m s$^{-1}$ at $t=0$. The graph shows its height $h$ against time $t$.

Sketch a graph showing the variation of $h$ with the horizontal distance $x$ (no values required).
questions.answer: Since $x=u\cos\theta\,t$ is proportional to $t$, the graph is the same shape: a symmetrical, concave-down parabola from the origin back to $h=0$.

questions.question:
A bullet is fired at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal with speed $200$ m s$^{-1}$ at $t=0$. The graph shows its height $h$ against time $t$.

State an expression for the initial vertical component of velocity $u_y$ in terms of the initial speed and $\theta$.
questions.answer: $u_y=200\sin\theta$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
A bullet is fired at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal with speed $200$ m s$^{-1}$ at $t=0$. The graph shows its height $h$ against time $t$.

Use data from the graph to deduce that $\theta=30^\circ$.
questions.answer:
From the graph the maximum height (about 500 m) is reached at $t=10$ s, where $v_y=0$.

$0=200\sin\theta-9.8\times10$, so $\sin\theta=0.49$ and $\theta=29.3^\circ\approx30^\circ$.

questions.question:
The probe Cassini is between Saturn and Jupiter, $3.9\times10^{11}$ m from Saturn and $4.2\times10^{11}$ m from Jupiter, on the line joining them. Mass of Cassini $2.2\times10^3$ kg, Saturn $5.7\times10^{26}$ kg, Jupiter $1.9\times10^{27}$ kg; a Saturn day is 10.7 hours.

Calculate the magnitude of the total gravitational field strength experienced by Cassini, ignoring the Sun.

The probe Cassini is between Saturn and Jupiter, $3.9\times10^{11}$ m from Saturn and $4.2\times10^{11}$ m from Jupiter, on the line joining them. Mass of Cassini $2.2\times10^3$ kg, Saturn $5.7\times10^{26}$ kg, Jupiter $1.9\times10^{27}$ kg; a Saturn day is 10.7 hours.

State the direction of the total gravitational field strength at Cassini.
questions.answer:
Towards Jupiter, since $g_J>g_S$.

*Note: the school's marking guideline says towards Saturn, which contradicts its own calculation.*

questions.question:
The probe Cassini is between Saturn and Jupiter, $3.9\times10^{11}$ m from Saturn and $4.2\times10^{11}$ m from Jupiter, on the line joining them. Mass of Cassini $2.2\times10^3$ kg, Saturn $5.7\times10^{26}$ kg, Jupiter $1.9\times10^{27}$ kg; a Saturn day is 10.7 hours.

Cassini is later to remain above the same point on Saturn's equator (a 'stationary' orbit). What is the period of this orbit in seconds?
questions.answer: The period equals one Saturn day: $10.7\times3600=3.85\times10^4$ s.

questions.question: Draw and label the forces acting on a car of mass $m$ moving around a banked track inclined at $\theta$: (i) with no friction; (ii) with friction.
questions.answer:
**(i)** Weight $mg$ vertically down, and the normal force $N$ perpendicular to the track. Their resultant is horizontal, towards the centre ($N\sin\theta$).

**(ii)** $mg$, $N$, and friction $f$ parallel to the track: down the slope (towards the centre) if the car is faster than the design speed, or up the slope if slower. The resultant is still horizontal towards the centre.

questions.question: A road with a turn of radius 125 m is designed for a speed of 18.0 m s$^{-1}$. At what angle should the turn be banked?
questions.answer:
With no friction needed: $N\cos\theta=mg$ and $N\sin\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

$\tan\theta=\dfrac{v^2}{rg}=\dfrac{18.0^2}{125\times9.8}=0.2645$, so $\theta=14.8^\circ$.

*Note: the school's solution solves for a speed instead of the banking angle.*

questions.question: The Hubble space telescope is in a circular orbit near the Earth and travels around the Earth once every 97 minutes. Calculate its angular speed.
questions.answer: $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{97\times60}=1.08\times10^{-3}$ rad s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: The Hubble space telescope is in a circular orbit near the Earth and travels around the Earth once every 97 minutes. Given $\omega=v/r$, calculate the radius of the orbit.
questions.answer:
Gravity provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}=m\omega^2r$, so

$r=\left(\dfrac{GM}{\omega^2}\right)^{1/3}=\left(\dfrac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times6.0\times10^{24}}{(1.08\times10^{-3})^2}\right)^{1/3}=7.0\times10^6$ m.

questions.question: The Hubble space telescope is in a circular orbit near the Earth and travels around the Earth once every 97 minutes. Its mass is $1.1\times10^4$ kg and its orbit radius is $7.0\times10^6$ m. Calculate the magnitude of the centripetal force acting on it.
questions.answer: $F=m\omega^2r=1.1\times10^4\times(1.08\times10^{-3})^2\times7.0\times10^6=9.0\times10^4$ N.

questions.question: Both Niels Bohr and de Broglie contributed to developing a model of the atom. By analysing the evidence, justify the acceptance of de Broglie's model of the atom instead of Bohr's model at that time.
questions.answer:
**Bohr (1913):** electrons occupy only certain stationary orbits without radiating; angular momentum is quantised, $mvr=nh/2\pi$; a photon with $hf=E_i-E_f$ is emitted or absorbed in a transition. It fixed the instability of Rutherford's atom and predicted the hydrogen spectral lines (Rydberg formula).

**Limitations:** the postulates were imposed without explanation (why are those orbits stable?); it worked only for one-electron species; it could not explain relative line intensities, the Zeeman effect or hyperfine structure; it mixed classical and quantum ideas.

**de Broglie (1924):** matter has wave properties, $\lambda=h/mv$. An electron in an atom forms a standing wave, so only orbits with $2\pi r=n\lambda$ are stable; other wavelengths interfere destructively. Substituting $\lambda=h/mv$ gives $mvr=nh/2\pi$, so Bohr's quantisation condition follows from a physical principle instead of being assumed.

**Evidence:** Davisson and Germer (1927) scattered electrons from a nickel crystal and found intensity maxima whose angles gave a wavelength matching $h/mv$; G. P. Thomson observed electron diffraction rings through thin films. Diffraction is a wave property, directly confirming matter waves.

**Justification:** de Broglie's model reproduced Bohr's successful predictions, explained why the energy levels are quantised, and its central hypothesis was verified experimentally. It also led to Schrödinger's wave mechanics, which handles more complex atoms and line intensities. It was therefore accepted as the better model, although it was itself only a step towards the quantum mechanical atom.

questions.question: Calculate the average binding energy per nucleon of $^{56}_{26}$Fe, given the mass of $^{56}$Fe is 55.934940 u, the mass of a proton (hydrogen atom) is 1.007825 u and the mass of a neutron is 1.008665 u.
questions.answer:
$\Delta m=26(1.007825)+30(1.008665)-55.934940=0.528460$ u

$E_B=0.528460\times931.5=492.3$ MeV, so per nucleon $=492.3/56=8.79$ MeV.

*Note: the paper misprints the proton mass as 0.997825 u (corrected above), and the school's answer of 8.55 MeV uses inconsistent values.*

questions.question: Analyse, with TWO suitable examples, how sustained and controlled amounts of energy can be produced from nuclear reactions.
questions.answer:
In both examples the products have less mass than the reactants (higher binding energy per nucleon), releasing $E=\Delta mc^2$. A steady output needs a reaction rate that regulates itself or is regulated.

**Fission reactor:** a slow neutron splits $^{235}$U into two smaller nuclei plus 2–3 neutrons, which can cause further fissions. A moderator slows neutrons so they are more likely to be captured; control rods absorb surplus neutrons so that on average exactly one neutron per fission causes another. The chain reaction is then critical: sustained at a constant power. Coolant removes the heat to raise steam.

**Fusion in a main sequence star:** hydrogen fuses to helium (proton–proton chain or CNO cycle) at very high temperature and density, which let nuclei overcome electrostatic repulsion. Gravity confines the plasma and balances thermal and radiation pressure. If the rate rises the core expands and cools, slowing fusion, and vice versa, giving a stable output for billions of years.

questions.question:
Crookes' discharge tube has a metal cross inside it. When a high voltage is applied, the glass behind the cross fluoresces and a shadow of the cross appears.

Explain how this shadow is formed.
questions.answer: Cathode rays leave the cathode and travel in straight lines through the evacuated tube. Those striking the cross are blocked; those passing it hit the glass and make it fluoresce. The region behind the cross receives no rays, so appears as a shadow.

questions.question:
Crookes' discharge tube has a metal cross inside it. When a high voltage is applied, the glass behind the cross fluoresces and a shadow of the cross appears.

When a magnet is moved towards the tube, the shadow moves across the glass. Explain this observation.
questions.answer: Cathode rays are moving charged particles (electrons), so a magnetic field exerts a force $F=qvB\sin\theta$ on them perpendicular to their velocity and the field. This deflects the beam, so the shadow shifts.

questions.question: State ONE way in which work involving gas discharge tubes contributed to the understanding of atomic structure.
questions.answer: Thomson used crossed electric and magnetic fields on cathode rays to measure the charge-to-mass ratio of the particles. It was the same for every cathode material and gas and far larger than that of a hydrogen ion, showing that atoms contain much lighter negative particles (electrons) and so are divisible.

questions.question:
Emily investigates the photoelectric effect with a light source, filters and a photocell. For each frequency she adjusts the reverse voltage until the current just reaches zero.

| Frequency ($\times10^{14}$ Hz) | 6.0 | 7.0 | 8.0 | 9.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Voltage (V) | 0.16 | 0.52 | 0.88 | 1.20 |

Plot the data and draw the graph of voltage ($-2$ to $2$ V) against frequency ($0$ to $10\times10^{14}$ Hz).
questions.answer: Plot the four points, draw the line of best fit and extrapolate it to cut both axes ($f$-intercept about $5.5\times10^{14}$ Hz, $V$-intercept about $-1.9$ V).

questions.question:
Emily investigates the photoelectric effect with a light source, filters and a photocell. For each frequency she adjusts the reverse voltage until the current just reaches zero.

| Frequency ($\times10^{14}$ Hz) | 6.0 | 7.0 | 8.0 | 9.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Voltage (V) | 0.16 | 0.52 | 0.88 | 1.20 |

From the graph, determine Planck's constant (in eV s), the threshold frequency and the work function of the metal (in eV).
questions.answer:
$eV_s=hf-\phi$, so $V_s=\dfrac{h}{e}f-\dfrac{\phi}{e}$.

Gradient $\approx3.5\times10^{-15}$ V s, so $h\approx3.5\times10^{-15}$ eV s.

Threshold frequency ($f$-intercept) $\approx5.5\times10^{14}$ Hz.

Work function ($V$-intercept magnitude) $\approx1.9$ eV.

questions.question: Outline the contributions of Newton and Huygens to the development of the model of light, and analyse the subsequent experimental evidence that supported the wave model of light.
questions.answer:
**Newton (corpuscular model):** light is a stream of tiny particles travelling in straight lines. Reflection is an elastic rebound. Refraction occurs because particles are attracted into a denser medium, increasing the normal velocity component, so it predicted light travels **faster** in water.

**Huygens (wave model):** every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets and the new wavefront is their envelope (he assumed longitudinal waves). This explains reflection and refraction, the latter requiring light to travel **slower** in a denser medium.

**Evidence:**

- **Young's double slit (1801):** alternating bright and dark fringes arise from constructive and destructive interference, which particles cannot explain.
- **Diffraction and the Poisson (Arago) spot:** Fresnel's wave theory predicted a bright spot at the centre of the shadow of a disc; Arago observed it.
- **Polarisation:** intensity through two polarisers follows Malus' law. This is explained only by transverse waves, which modified Huygens' model.
- **Foucault (1850), with Fizeau:** light travels more slowly in water than in air, contradicting Newton's prediction and agreeing with Huygens.

Together these showed interference, diffraction and polarisation are wave behaviour and refuted a key particle prediction, so the wave model was accepted until the photoelectric effect required a quantum description.

questions.question: Describe how the spectrum of a star can be used to determine its temperature and chemical composition.
questions.answer:
**Temperature:** a star radiates approximately as a black body. Measure the intensity against wavelength, find the peak wavelength $\lambda_{max}$ and apply Wien's law $T=b/\lambda_{max}$. Hotter stars peak at shorter wavelengths.

**Composition:** cooler gases in the star's atmosphere absorb photons whose energies match their electron transitions, producing dark absorption lines on the continuous spectrum. Each element has a unique set of lines, so matching them with laboratory emission or absorption spectra identifies the elements present.

questions.question: Outline TWO pieces of evidence that quantitatively support time dilation.
questions.answer:
**Muons (Rossi–Hall, 1941):** cosmic rays create muons high in the atmosphere. Muon counts were compared on a mountain and lower down. With their short rest half-life (about 1.5 μs), few should survive the trip, but far more did, in agreement with the dilated half-life predicted for their speed.

**Hafele–Keating (1971):** caesium atomic clocks were flown eastwards and westwards around the world and compared with ground clocks. The eastbound clocks lost time and the westbound clocks gained time, matching the predicted combination of velocity (special) and gravitational (general) time dilation. Relative to a non-rotating frame, the eastbound clock moved fastest and ran slowest.

(Also acceptable: transition frequencies of fast ions in accelerators.)

*Note: the school's sample answer says both flown clocks recorded less time; the westbound clocks actually gained time.*

questions.question:
In a simplified mass spectrometer, charged particles are accelerated through 3000 V (Stage 1), then enter a 0.5 T magnetic field (Stage 2) perpendicular to their velocity and move in a circular arc.

Show that a proton accelerated in Stage 1 emerges with a speed of $7.6\times10^5$ m s$^{-1}$.

In a simplified mass spectrometer, charged particles are accelerated through 3000 V (Stage 1), then enter a 0.5 T magnetic field (Stage 2) perpendicular to their velocity and move in a circular arc.

Determine the radius of the path of this proton (speed $7.6\times10^5$ m s$^{-1}$) in the magnetic field.
questions.answer: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}=\dfrac{1.673\times10^{-27}\times7.6\times10^5}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.5}=1.6\times10^{-2}$ m.

questions.question:
In a simplified mass spectrometer, charged particles are accelerated through 3000 V (Stage 1), then enter a 0.5 T magnetic field (Stage 2) perpendicular to their velocity and move in a circular arc.

A mixture of protons and singly ionised deuterium (twice the proton's mass, same charge) is accelerated and enters Stage 2. Find an exact expression for the ratio $r_D/r_P$ of the radii of curvature.
questions.answer:
$v=\sqrt{2qV/m}$, so $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2mqV}}{qB}\propto\sqrt m$.

$\dfrac{r_D}{r_P}=\sqrt2$.

questions.question:
A horizontal wire of length 0.8 cm, perpendicular to the field between two neodymium magnets, is connected to a variable supply and ammeter. The wire is supported by a plastic box on a set of scales; the magnets are supported separately. The graph shows the scale reading against current (line of best fit: slope 0.1566 g A$^{-1}$, intercept 55.77 g).

Explain why the $y$-intercept is not zero even though the current is zero.
questions.answer: The scales were not zeroed: with no current they still read the mass of the box and wire resting on them (55.77 g).

questions.question:
A horizontal wire of length 0.8 cm, perpendicular to the field between two neodymium magnets, is connected to a variable supply and ammeter. The wire is supported by a plastic box on a set of scales; the magnets are supported separately. The graph shows the scale reading against current (line of best fit: slope 0.1566 g A$^{-1}$, intercept 55.77 g).

Using a diagram and a relevant equation, explain why the scale reading increases as the current increases.
questions.answer:
The current-carrying wire in the field experiences $F=BIL\sin\theta$ with $\theta=90^\circ$, so $F=BIL\propto I$. The current and field directions are such that $F$ on the wire is downwards.

Forces on the box and wire: $N$ (up) $=mg+BIL$ (both down). The scales read $N$, so the reading increases linearly with $I$.

questions.question:
A horizontal wire of length 0.8 cm, perpendicular to the field between two neodymium magnets, is connected to a variable supply and ammeter. The wire is supported by a plastic box on a set of scales; the magnets are supported separately. The graph shows the scale reading against current (line of best fit: slope 0.1566 g A$^{-1}$, intercept 55.77 g).

By what factor should the vertical axis (in grams) be multiplied so that it gives the upward force exerted by the scale in newtons?
questions.answer: $9.8\times10^{-3}$ (g to kg, then multiply by $g$).

questions.question:
A horizontal wire of length 0.8 cm, perpendicular to the field between two neodymium magnets, is connected to a variable supply and ammeter. The wire is supported by a plastic box on a set of scales; the magnets are supported separately. The graph shows the scale reading against current (line of best fit: slope 0.1566 g A$^{-1}$, intercept 55.77 g).

Use the gradient of the line of best fit to determine the magnetic field strength between the magnets.

A student has a power supply with AC and DC outputs, an iron core, AC and DC voltmeters and ammeters, coils of 300 turns and 600 turns, and connecting wires. Draw a labelled diagram of an experimental set-up to demonstrate the operation of a step-up transformer.
questions.answer: Connect the AC output to the 300-turn primary and place the 600-turn secondary on the same iron core. Connect an AC voltmeter in parallel across each coil; the secondary voltage should be greater than the primary (ideally double).

questions.question: Using equations, explain how Faraday's law applies to the operation of an ideal transformer.
questions.answer:
Alternating current in the primary produces a changing flux in the core. By Faraday's law $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$.

In an ideal transformer the same $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$ links both coils, so $V_p=N_p\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ and $V_s=N_s\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ in magnitude, giving $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}$.

questions.question: A student tests a step-up transformer (300-turn primary, 600-turn secondary on an iron core). Explain how and why the results would be expected to differ from those for an ideal transformer.
questions.answer: The measured secondary voltage (and output power) would be lower than ideal (less than twice the primary voltage). Not all primary flux links the secondary, and energy is lost as heat through coil resistance and eddy currents (and hysteresis) in the core.
